articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian 'Oil Trustees' and Issues Cuba FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals involved in Iran's illicit oil sales. Four Iranians were sanctioned for acting as "oil trustees," collecting proceeds from international oil sales to help Tehran evade sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade.

Among those designated are Mohammad Javad Bavand, identified as a former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, the brother of the Iranian Football Federation's president. These individuals are accused of retaining oil revenues for personal gain and facilitating the circumvention of sanctions.

In a separate action, OFAC also issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba sanctions. This guidance aims to clarify existing regulations and assist entities in complying with U.S. restrictions concerning transactions with Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Amends Russia GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations under its counter narcotics and cyber-related sanctions authorities. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and malicious cyber activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing certain authorizations for transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. This aims to ensure that legitimate activities are not unduly impacted by the new sanctions.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated its Frequently Asked Questions concerning Russia sanctions. This amendment likely provides further clarity or adjustments to existing restrictions in response to ongoing developments related to Russia's actions.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has implemented new counter terrorism designations. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting or engaging in acts of terrorism, aiming to disrupt their financial networks and operations globally.

The designations fall under OFAC's broader efforts to combat international terrorism and protect the U.S. financial system from illicit activities. These measures typically involve freezing assets and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the reasons for their inclusion on the sanctions list, are expected to be outlined in accompanying guidance from OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations

The designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of these organizations, preventing them from engaging in activities that threaten international security and stability. Such measures typically include asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.
These combined designations underscore the interconnected nature of various illicit activities and the U.S. commitment to employing a broad range of tools to combat them.

body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a significant round of designations, targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and malicious cyber activities globally.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also implemented new designations related to Cuba. These designations, made pursuant to Executive Order 14404, target actors involved in Cuba's oil transportation networks, state-owned enterprises, and government elites.

Additionally, OFAC published a Cuba-related Determination, which extends the order's sectoral designation authority to Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors. This determination provides a basis for future designations of foreign persons operating in these sectors, further expanding the scope of U.S. sanctions on Cuba.

The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite saw steep losses, dropping 5.28% and erasing all its gains for the year, with the S&P 500 also falling 3.7%. This sell-off intensified despite Anthropic's record IPO debut, as investors continued to reassess the macroeconomic environment.

Concerns about elevated valuations, profitability, and the sustainability of investment spending in the AI sector contributed to the market mood shifting from 'buying the dip' to questioning the extent of the correction. Nvidia shares also fell after California launched an investigation into its advanced semiconductors potentially ending up in China.

articles.headline: Ebola Cases More Than Double in DR Congo, WHO Reports
body: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has more than doubled in three months, with over 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths reported across 67 health zones in eight provinces. The head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, highlighted the severe impact on children, who account for over a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths.

Seven out of ten children under five with confirmed Ebola have died, underscoring the devastating toll on the youngest population. The WHO Director-General made these remarks at the third meeting of WHO's Emergency Committee on the Bundibugyo virus disease epidemic.

The escalating crisis in the DRC continues to pose significant challenges for public health efforts and humanitarian response, requiring urgent international attention and resources to contain the spread and provide care to affected communities.

articles.headline: COP31 Ends Without Climate Pact Amid Divisions Over Fossil Fuels
body: The COP31 climate summit concluded on November 22, 2026, without a climate pact, as negotiators failed to bridge divisions over fossil fuels. UN Secretary-General António Guterres described the outcome as a “deeply disappointing” setback, emphasizing that the failure to reach consensus does not alter the realities of the climate crisis.

Despite two weeks of talks and two days of overtime in Antalya, Türkiye, governments could not agree on the summit's main political decisions. Guterres warned that global temperatures continue to break records, climate impacts are intensifying, and greenhouse gas emissions remain dangerously high, putting the world on course to exceed the 1.5°C warming limit.

UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell acknowledged the frustration of delegates and urged countries to learn lessons from Antalya, stating that “the world cannot afford a repeat of this moment.” He stressed that fossil fuels remain the primary driver of global warming and cautioned against efforts to delay the transition to cleaner energy.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued an interim final rule, effective November 19, 2026, expanding export controls related to advanced computing items. This rule, titled “Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,” aims to prevent circumvention of existing restrictions on access to sensitive U.S. technology through remote computing arrangements, including cloud services, offered by data centers in third countries.

The new rule imposes a license requirement for exports, reexports, and transfers (in-country) of advanced computing items where there is "knowledge" that the item is destined to a data center, wherever located, that provides access to a significant volume of compute power to or for companies headquartered in China (including Hong Kong and Macau) or a destination specified in Country Group D:5. It also adds a new license requirement for advanced chips and other computing items to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, which BIS views as presenting an "unacceptable risk of diversion."

The IFR formally rescinds the never-enforced Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule and clarifies that providing remote access to these items is now treated as a restricted end use when the recipient is headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination. Affected data center operators have 90 days from publication to obtain a BIS license to continue providing cloud compute services to these customers. Following the rule, TSMC is reportedly restricting Chinese chip designers and suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders.
articles.source: Federal Register / Simpson Thacher / Gibson Dunn / DLA Piper / K&L Gates

articles.headline: Andhra Pradesh Amends Semiconductor Policy, Offers Up to 80% Support for Silicon Fabs
body: The Andhra Pradesh government has amended its Semiconductor and Display Fab Policy 4.0 to align with the second phase of the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM 2.0). The amendment, notified on November 16, 2026, offers state incentives that match Union support for various project categories.

Under the revised policy, silicon fabrication projects are eligible for combined Union and State incentives of up to 80% of eligible capital costs, with each government contributing 40%. Compound semiconductor, photonics, sensor, discrete semiconductor, and display fabrication projects, along with advanced packaging units, will receive up to 70% combined support.

The amended policy also extends support to chip design, machinery, materials, research, and talent development. The state plans to establish a 5,000-acre AP Semiconductor Park in Tirupati to host manufacturers and suppliers, providing developed land, shared cleanrooms, and essential utilities.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
